lessons.title: The 2000s Moderation: How Formal Inflation Targeting Changed the RBI's Playbook

children.text: After the pain of 1991, India had close to its best two decades of growth. But the formal 4% inflation target you met in Chapter 1, with its clearly defined tolerance band and a committee that has to explain itself if it misses, did not exist until 2016. It was not born out of the 1991 crisis at all. It was born out of a second, homegrown inflation crisis roughly two decades later, one that made policymakers conclude that a discretionary, take-it-case-by-case approach to monetary policy was no longer good enough.

body.text: India's formal inflation-targeting framework was not a theoretical upgrade adopted in calm times. It was a direct policy response to a painful, multi-year episode of double-digit inflation in the early 2010s that convinced the government and the RBI that a legally binding target, not just good judgment, was needed to anchor expectations.

children.text: From Crisis Management to the Multiple Indicator Approach

Through most of the 1990s, the RBI leaned on a fairly narrow monetary targeting approach inherited from the pre-1991 era. In 1998, under Governor Bimal Jalan, it formally shifted to what became known as the Multiple Indicator Approach (MIA): rather than anchoring policy to a single number, the RBI weighed a broad basket of signals together, money supply growth, credit growth, output, the fiscal position, trade and capital flows, and inflation among them, and used judgment to set policy. This gave the RBI real flexibility. It also gave it no hard, publicly stated number to be held accountable to, a gap that mattered enormously a decade later.
The 2000s Boom, and Its Hidden Cost

The mid-2000s were, by most measures, India's strongest sustained growth run since independence, with GDP growth touching close to 9% a year for several years running, inflation relatively contained, and the Sensex and Nifty on a multi-year bull run. The 2008 Global Financial Crisis interrupted this, though India's relatively closed capital account and conservative banking regulation meant it weathered the shock far better than the US or Europe. The RBI and the government responded with aggressive rate cuts and fiscal stimulus, and growth recovered quickly. That fast, stimulus-driven recovery, arriving while global commodity prices were also climbing, is what set up the next crisis: an overheating economy running into supply-side constraints, particularly in food and fuel.

stats.label: Formal Target, Adopted 2016
stats.context: The framework this episode ultimately produced

body.text: The 2010-13 period was politically brutal. CPI inflation ran near or above double digits for stretches of several years, driven heavily by food prices, and household anger over the cost of daily essentials became a major political issue. The RBI, under Governor D. Subbarao, raised rates repeatedly through this period, but with limited success, because a meaningful share of the pressure was coming from supply-side and structural sources that interest rates alone could not fix, echoing the cost-push and supply-constraint lessons from earlier in this course.

children.text: The Urjit Patel Committee and the Case for a Hard Target

By 2013-14, it was clear to policymakers that the Multiple Indicator Approach's flexibility had come at a real cost: without a stated numerical target, the RBI had no external anchor forcing it to act early, and the public had no clear yardstick to judge whether policy was on track. The RBI set up a committee headed by Urjit Patel, then Deputy Governor, to review the framework. Its central recommendation, delivered in January 2014, was to formally adopt CPI, not WPI, as India's nominal anchor, to set an explicit numerical inflation target, and to move policy decisions from the sole discretion of the RBI Governor to a Monetary Policy Committee with a mix of RBI and external, government-appointed members.

body.title: From Discretion to a Legal Target

events.title: Multiple Indicator Approach Adopted
events.description: The RBI under Bimal Jalan moves to weighing a broad basket of indicators rather than a single monetary target, gaining flexibility but no hard accountability benchmark.

events.title: Global Financial Crisis and Stimulus
events.description: India weathers the GFC comparatively well but responds with aggressive rate cuts and fiscal stimulus, setting the stage for an overheating economy once growth resumes.

events.title: Double-Digit Inflation Takes Hold
events.description: CPI inflation runs near or above double digits for extended stretches, driven heavily by food prices, becoming a defining economic and political problem of the period.

events.title: The Urjit Patel Committee Reports
events.description: The committee recommends CPI as the nominal anchor, a formal numerical inflation target, and a Monetary Policy Committee to replace sole Governor discretion.

events.title: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement
events.description: The Government of India and the RBI formally agree to the inflation-targeting framework and the 4% target with a tolerance band, ahead of the legal amendment.

events.title: The RBI Act Is Amended
events.description: Parliament amends the RBI Act to legally mandate flexible inflation targeting and formally establish the six-member Monetary Policy Committee, the framework operating today.

body.label: The Accountability Clause
body.context: If average inflation stays outside the 2% to 6% tolerance band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI is legally required to send the government a report explaining why, and what it will do about it, and by when. This single clause is what turns the 4% target from a soft aspiration into genuine accountability.

body.title: Discretionary MIA vs. Formal Inflation Targeting

columns.label: Multiple Indicator Approach (1998-2016)
points: No single stated numerical inflation target
Policy decisions rested on the RBI Governor's discretion
Flexible, but hard for the public or markets to hold accountable
WPI carried significant weight alongside CPI

columns.label: Formal Inflation Targeting (2016-present)
points: Legally mandated CPI target of 4%, with a 2% to 6% band
Decisions made by a 6-member Monetary Policy Committee, minutes published
A missed target for 3 consecutive quarters forces a public accountability report
CPI is the sole official nominal anchor

body.title: Why a Legal Target Anchors Expectations
body.scenario: Under the old Multiple Indicator Approach, the RBI could, in principle, tolerate elevated inflation for a while without ever having to publicly justify it in a structured way. Under the post-2016 framework, if inflation drifts outside the band for three quarters, the RBI must formally explain itself to the government.
body.prompt: Recall the Volcker lesson from Chapter 2: credibility, not just the policy mechanism itself, is what actually anchors inflation expectations. Explain why a legally mandated target with a public accountability clause does more to anchor expectations than the same RBI simply promising to act sensibly using its own discretion.
body.modelAnswer: A discretionary promise is only as credible as the institution's track record and the public's trust that it will not quietly relax its stance under political or economic pressure, exactly the credibility problem that undermined Arthur Burns' Fed in the 1970s. A legal target with a binding accountability clause changes the incentive structure: the RBI cannot simply let inflation run without consequence, because doing so triggers a mandatory public explanation. Households, businesses and markets can then form expectations based on a known, enforceable rule rather than trusting an individual policymaker's judgment, which is precisely the kind of durable credibility Volcker had to build through a recession, but which India's framework now builds into the law itself.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What was the single most direct trigger for India moving to a legally mandated inflation target in 2016?
options: A multi-year episode of double-digit CPI inflation in the early 2010s that discretionary policy struggled to control
A recommendation from the IMF as a condition of a 1991 loan
body.explanation: The 1991 crisis dismantled the License Raj, not the RBI's monetary framework. The push for a hard, legal inflation target came specifically from the 2010-13 double-digit inflation episode and the resulting Urjit Patel Committee review, roughly two decades later.

points: India's formal 4% inflation-targeting framework, introduced in 2016, was a direct response to the 2010-13 double-digit CPI inflation episode, not the 1991 crisis.
The pre-2016 Multiple Indicator Approach gave the RBI flexibility but no hard, publicly stated target, which made it difficult to hold policy accountable when inflation ran high.
The Urjit Patel Committee's 2014 recommendations, CPI as the nominal anchor, a numerical target, and a Monetary Policy Committee, became law through the 2016 RBI Act amendment.
The 3-consecutive-quarters accountability clause is what turns the 4% target from an aspiration into an enforceable commitment, echoing the credibility lessons from the Volcker chapter.
The next chapter picks up an event that sits right inside this same window, the 2013 taper tantrum, one of the acute shocks that added urgency to this reform.
